pins.title: Heidi's Alp
pins.text: Isao Takahata, Hayao Miyazaki and Yōichi Kotabe spent about ten days scouting Switzerland and Germany for Heidi, Girl of the Alps, two of them in the village of Maienfeld. It was a pioneering trip for TV animation. The mountain hut they sketched is now marketed to visitors as “Heidi's Alp”, and the series became a staple of European childhoods.

pins.title: Astro Boy crosses the Pacific
pins.text: NBC Enterprises syndicated an English version of Tetsuwan Atom in 1963, the same year it premiered in Japan, with the characters given American names. Kimba the White Lion (1966) and Speed Racer (1967) followed, and most young viewers had no idea the shows came from Japan.

pins.title: Goldrake
pins.text: Public broadcaster RAI aired UFO Robot Grendizer as Goldrake in 1978. Italy's new private channels then filled their schedules with Japanese series, and Candy Candy, Lady Oscar (The Rose of Versailles) and Holly e Benji (Captain Tsubasa) became shared Italian memories.

pins.title: Goldorak
pins.text: Antenne 2 began showing Grendizer as Goldorak in July 1978. By January 1979 it was on the cover of Paris Match, and critics were warning about its influence on children. By 1990 more than a third of the animation on French television was Japanese.

pins.title: Grendizer
pins.text: Dubbed into Arabic in Lebanon during the civil war, with Jihad Al-Atrash as the exiled prince Duke Fleed, Grendizer spread across the Arab world. Its story of a displaced hero defending a home that is not his own struck a deep chord, and the show remains a shared reference for several generations.

pins.title: Voltes V is pulled off the air
pins.text: Ferdinand Marcos's government took Voltes V and other robot shows off television four episodes before the end, officially for violence. Many viewers believed the real reason was its story of an uprising against a tyrant. It returned after the 1986 People Power Revolution, and the final episodes were not broadcast until 1999.

pins.title: Astro Boy on CCTV
pins.text: China Central Television broadcast Astro Boy in December 1980, early in the reform era. Ikkyū-san followed in 1983 and was rerun so often that schoolchildren memorised its Japanese theme song.

pins.title: Oliver y Benji
pins.text: Captain Tsubasa became Oliver y Benji in Spanish, Olive et Tom in French and Holly e Benji in Italian. A generation of professional footballers has credited it. Fernando Torres said he took up the game because of it: “I wanted to be Oliver.”

pins.title: Akira on VHS
pins.text: Island World released Akira on video in Britain in 1991. The label renamed itself Manga Entertainment in 1993, and for a decade its violent, adult catalogue was what many British viewers thought anime was.

pins.title: A Japanese Ramayana
pins.text: Documentary maker Yugo Sako spent nearly a decade making Ramayana: The Legend of Prince Rama with the Indian animator Ram Mohan. Objections to a Japanese company adapting India's epic kept it from wide release, but it later found a large audience through Cartoon Network in India.

pins.title: Os Cavaleiros do Zodíaco
pins.text: Rede Manchete got Saint Seiya free in exchange for airing commercials for Bandai's toys. It became a national phenomenon and opened the door for Dragon Ball, Sailor Moon and the anime that followed. Brazil also has the largest Japanese diaspora in the world.

pins.title: The ban comes down
pins.text: South Korea lifted its postwar ban on Japanese cultural imports in four stages between October 1998 and January 2004. In 2023 The First Slam Dunk sold more than three million tickets there and stayed in cinemas for almost a year.

pins.title: Goku versus Jiren in the town square
pins.text: When Dragon Ball Super episode 130 aired, city governments put it on big screens. About 15,000 people gathered in Ciudad Juárez and more than 10,000 in Machala, Ecuador. Toei said it had not authorised the screenings.

pins.title: Hamtaro at Democracy Monument
pins.text: Pro-democracy protesters ran circles around Democracy Monument singing a parody of the Hamtaro theme. “The most delicious thing is sunflower seeds” became “the most delicious thing is the people's taxes”.

pins.title: The Straw Hat flag
pins.text: Ahead of Independence Day, Indonesians flew the Jolly Roger of One Piece's Straw Hat Pirates in place of the national flag, as a protest against the government. Within weeks the flag was being carried by young protesters in other countries.

pins.title: Gen Z under a pirate flag
pins.text: The Straw Hat flag flew over the youth protests that brought down Nepal's government. For Rohan Rai, 19, it stood for “freedom, loyalty and defiance against injustice”. It appeared again in Madagascar, the Philippines, Peru and elsewhere.

pins.title: Grendizer comes home to its fans
pins.text: Half a century after the Arabic dub, Saudi Arabia's Manga Productions co-developed and marketed Grendizer U, a new series built for the audience that had grown up with the original.

pins.title: From Pokémon to KPop Demon Hunters
pins.text: Pokémon: The First Movie opened at No. 1 in November 1999 and earned $85.7 million, a record for anime in North America that stood until 2025, when Infinity Castle opened to $70.6 million and went on to pass it. In 2026 the Oscar for animated feature went to KPop Demon Hunters, an American film whose directors named Sailor Moon, Cowboy Bebop and FLCL among their models.
